4.9 Performance Evaluation

Risk-adjusted returns

Section titled “Risk-adjusted returns”

One fund returned 15% last year and another 10%. Is the first one necessarily better? Not necessarily: the first may have taken far more risk. Evaluating performance means looking at risk-adjusted returns. Let the fund’s average return be Rˉp\bar R_pRˉp​ and the risk-free rate rfr_frf​:

  • The Sharpe ratio (Sharpe ratio, Sharpe, 1966): Sp=Rˉp−rfσpS_p = \frac{\bar R_p - r_f}{\sigma_p}Sp​=σp​Rˉp​−rf​​, the excess return per unit of total risk.
  • The Treynor ratio (Treynor, 1965): Tp=Rˉp−rfβpT_p = \frac{\bar R_p - r_f}{\beta_p}Tp​=βp​Rˉp​−rf​​, the excess return per unit of systematic risk.
  • Jensen’s alpha (Jensen, 1968): αp=Rˉp−[rf+βp(RˉM−rf)]\alpha_p = \bar R_p - [r_f + \beta_p(\bar R_M - r_f)]αp​=Rˉp​−[rf​+βp​(RˉM​−rf​)], the part of the actual return above the security market line (alpha), usually estimated by the intercept of a regression.
  • The information ratio: IRp=αpσ(ep)IR_p = \frac{\alpha_p}{\sigma(e_p)}IRp​=σ(ep​)αp​​, alpha divided by the standard deviation of the residual, that is, the alpha earned per unit of firm-specific risk. It is also often computed as the average return over a benchmark divided by the tracking error (the standard deviation of the difference from the benchmark’s return).

To make the Sharpe ratio easier to read, Modigliani and Modigliani (1997) proposed M²: combine the fund with the risk-free asset in the proportion that gives it the market’s volatility, then compare its return with the market’s, M2=rf+Sp σM−RˉMM^2 = r_f + S_p\,\sigma_M - \bar R_MM2=rf​+Sp​σM​−RˉM​.

Check C1
A fund borrows at the risk-free rate to double its position. Its Sharpe ratio doubles.
Think: with 2 times leverage, by what factors do the excess return Rˉp−rf\bar R_p - r_fRˉp​−rf​ and the standard deviation σp\sigma_pσp​ change?

Which measure to use

Section titled “Which measure to use”

The measures count different risks. Which one to use depends on the fund’s place in the investor’s total wealth, that is, on which part of the fund’s risk the investor actually bears.

Check C2
An investor holds only one stock fund plus the risk-free asset. Fund A: Sharpe ratio 0.45, Treynor ratio 6. Fund B: Sharpe ratio 0.38, Treynor ratio 9. In choosing, he should mainly look at:
The Treynor ratio counts only systematic risk. Does he hold other risky assets that would diversify the fund's firm-specific risk?
The two measures count different risks. Which risk does he actually bear?
The average return ignores risk. He can adjust his risk with the risk-free asset; what then determines the best risk–return combination he can get?

If the fund is only a small part of a well-diversified portfolio, most of its firm-specific risk is diversified away in the whole portfolio, and what matters is its beta and alpha: look at the Treynor ratio or Jensen’s alpha. If an active fund is added to a passive index portfolio, its alpha must be weighed against the firm-specific risk it adds: look at the information ratio. Treynor and Black (1973) showed that when the active fund is added in the best proportion, the portfolio’s Sharpe ratio satisfies S2=SM2+IR2S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2S2=SM2​+IR2 (Exercises Question 1).

The choice of benchmark matters just as much. 4.6 Multifactor Models showed that a fund tilted toward small value stocks shows an alpha by the CAPM, which may disappear with a three- or four-factor model (adding momentum). A fund’s benchmark should match its investment style; choosing a benchmark that is easy to beat makes performance look better than it is. Also, a manager’s timing (changing beta) and style drift during the period distort measures computed with a fixed beta.

Luck or skill

Section titled “Luck or skill”

Even with the right measure, there is a harder question: is the performance luck or skill? The estimation error of alpha is large (4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta). If a fund’s true information ratio is IRIRIR and alpha is estimated from TTT years of annual data, its t-value (t-statistic) is about

t≈IR×Tt \approx IR \times \sqrt{T}t≈IR×T​
Check C3
In Figure 2-1, raise the true information ratio from 0.3 to 0.6. The number of years needed for the expected t-value to reach 1.96:
The t-value is about IRTIR\sqrt{T}IRT​. When IR doubles, by what fraction must T\sqrt{T}T​ change to reach the same t-value? And T?
The threshold is still 1.96, but how fast the t-value grows has changed. Look at how the solid line changes.
Greater skill means a larger alpha relative to the noise each year. Does that make skill easier or harder to prove?

An information ratio of 0.5 is already considered very good active management, yet even then the expected t-value takes about 15 years to reach 1.96. And there are thousands of funds, some of which will have outstanding long records by chance even with no skill at all (multiple testing).

Check C4
If fund performance comes mainly from skill rather than luck, funds that did well in the past should tend to do better than other funds in the future too.
Think: which carries over to the next period, skill or luck?

The research findings: Carhart (1997) found that the funds with the best performance in one year are only slightly above average the next year, and the edge mostly disappears after fees and trading costs; the worst funds tend to stay bad, mainly because of high fees and high turnover. Fama and French (2010) used simulation to compare the distribution of alphas of US active stock funds with the distribution if none had skill, and found that after fees few funds have enough skill to cover their costs.

Survivorship bias

Section titled “Survivorship bias”

Funds that do badly are often closed or merged into other funds, disappearing from databases and from fund companies’ advertising. Historical performance computed only from surviving funds overstates how active management actually did; this is called survivorship bias. A similar problem is backfill bias: hedge funds join a database only after building a good record, and bring their earlier performance with them.

Fund companies also make use of this: a company that runs many funds advertises only its best ones and quietly merges away those that do badly. When looking at a fund’s record, ask how many funds it was picked from.

Check C5
A fund database includes only funds that are still operating. Using it to compute the average performance of active funds over the past 15 years gives a result that is:
Which funds are more likely to be closed or merged, those that did well or those that did badly?
Over 15 years a substantial share of funds is closed or merged. And even if the share were small, is their performance the same as that of the survivors?
Why do funds shrink and close? Are poor performance and outflows related?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The Sharpe ratio counts total risk, the Treynor ratio and Jensen’s alpha count systematic risk, and the information ratio relates alpha to firm-specific risk; M² turns the Sharpe ratio into a rate of return.
  • For a small part of a diversified portfolio use alpha or the Treynor ratio; for a fund added to an index portfolio use the information ratio, S2=SM2+IR2S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2S2=SM2​+IR2; the choice depends on which part of the risk the investor actually bears.
  • The benchmark should match the style; factor exposures can be mistaken for alpha.
  • The t-value of alpha is about IRTIR\sqrt{T}IRT​, so telling luck from skill needs a long record; performance persists only weakly.
  • Survivorship bias and selective advertising overstate the performance of active management.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
The market's expected return is 9% with a standard deviation of 16%, and the risk-free rate is 3%. Active fund P has an expected return of 12%, a standard deviation of 24% and a beta of 1.1.
(a) What are P's Sharpe ratio and Jensen's alpha? Compare with the market's Sharpe ratio.
(b) A colleague says: "P's Sharpe ratio is no higher than the market's, so buying some P in addition to an index fund will not improve the portfolio." Use P's information ratio and the Treynor–Black result S2=SM2+IR2S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2S2=SM2​+IR2 to evaluate this statement. How does the conclusion differ for an investor who holds only P?
Question 2
A news story says: "This fund manager has beaten her benchmark 10 years in a row. If it were luck, the chance of beating it in any year would be one half, and the chance of 10 years in a row less than one in a thousand, so she must have skill." There are 2,000 funds of this kind.
(a) Suppose no manager has skill, each beats the benchmark with a 50% chance each year, independently across years and funds. How many of the 2,000 funds would you expect to beat the benchmark 10 years in a row? What is the probability that at least one does?
(b) Over the 10 years she beat the benchmark by 2 percentage points a year on average, with a tracking error of 4 percentage points. What is the t-value of her excess return? Using (a), evaluate the story.
Question 3
A research firm says: "Over the past 15 years, US active stock funds returned 7.5% a year on average, against 6.5% for index funds, so active management beat the index by 1 percentage point a year on average." Its data include only surviving funds. In fact there were 100 such funds 15 years ago, of which 40 were closed or merged during the period, having returned 3% a year on average while they existed. For simplicity, average across funds with equal weights, giving every fund the same weight.
(a) Including all funds, what is the average annual return of active funds? By how many percentage points does survivorship bias overstate the average?
(b) Evaluate the research firm's statement. If an investor had picked an active fund at random 15 years ago, how would his expected result differ from what the firm says?
Question 4
A fund has a beta of 0.7. Its marketing says: "Last year the market fell 30% but we fell only 20%, proof of the manager's skill at controlling risk." For simplicity, assume a risk-free rate of 0.
(a) By the CAPM, how much should the fund have fallen last year? What is its Jensen's alpha?
(b) The year before, the market rose 35% and the fund rose 25%. What was that year's alpha? Evaluate the marketing claim. When would "falling less in down markets" show skill?
